1.e4 c5 2.f4.name: Sicilian Defence: McDonnell Attack
1.e4 c5 2.f4.background: The name McDonnell Attack stems from the 14th match game between Alexander McDonnell and Louis de La Bourdonnais, played in London in 1834 and won by Black. The line is also known as the Grand Prix Attack, after the weekend tournaments held in England in the 1970s.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 d5.strategy: Counterattacks in the centre before White's kingside play gets going: e4 is attacked and nothing defends it. Whatever White chooses, Black gets either a lead in development or a comfortable structure, which makes this the best reply to the immediate 2.f4.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6.strategy: A quiet, flexible reply: Black develops and eyes d4, ready to play as in any other Sicilian. It makes less of the loosening f-pawn advance than a strike in the centre does, so White keeps the attacking plan but Black has a normal game.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 e5.name: King's Gambit Declined: Mafia Defence
1.e4 c5 2.f4 e5.strategy: Pushes the pawn where it can be taken: 3.fxe5 wins it outright, as nothing can recapture on e5. Black has attacked the f-pawn, but White captures first and is a clean pawn up.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5.strategy: Takes the pawn and so accepts the gambit, the main line. White keeps it only briefly: Black wins it back with a lead in development, and White has to be ready to give it up for a solid position.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 d5 3.Nc3.name: Sicilian Defence: McDonnell Attack, Toilet Variation
1.e4 c5 2.f4 d5 3.Nc3.background: The 3.Nc3 way of declining the gambit is called the Toilet Variation, after its reputed place of invention.
1.e4 c5 2.f4 d5 3.Nc3.strategy: Declines the gambit by defending e4 with a developing move. The knight is a target, though: ...d4 drives it back and gains space for Black, so White's centre stays safe but Black is the one with the space.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 d5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops, but ignores the pawn tension: ...dxe4 wins a pawn with tempo, since the e4 pawn attacks the knight on f3 and it has to move again. White is a pawn down with little to show for it.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 Nf6.name: Sicilian Defence: McDonnell Attack, Tal Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 Nf6.background: Mikhail Tal pioneered the gambit, playing 3...Nf6 against Harston in 1979. Jeremy Silman and others count it as Black's best reply to 2.f4, which has made the immediate 2.f4 less popular.
1.e4 c5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 Nf6.strategy: The gambit idea: instead of retaking at once, Black attacks d5 a second time and plays for quick development. White can hold the pawn only awkwardly; once it falls, Black has the more active pieces against a position loosened by the f-pawn advance.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5.strategy: Restores the material at once and keeps a sound position, but the queen comes out early and Nc3 hits it with tempo. Black is fine, yet gives up the quicker development that the gambit offers against a kingside loosened by f4.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 e6.strategy: Hits the d5 pawn from the other side: if White takes on e6, ...Bxe6 develops the bishop with a lead for the pawn; if White develops instead, ...exd5 restores the material. White can simply take on e6, though, and Black must prove the lead is worth a pawn.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 d5 3.Nf3 dxe4.name: Bird's Opening: Dutch Variation, Batavo Gambit
1.e4 c5 2.f4 d5 3.Nf3 dxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn with tempo: the e4 pawn attacks the knight on f3, which has to move again. Black is a pawn up, and White's compensation, a lead in development, is thin.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 d5 3.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Adds a second attacker to e4 and develops, so White has to settle the tension at once. Black does not win a pawn, but gets a comfortable, harmonious development against a kingside already loosened by f4.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 d5 3.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops and adds pressure to the centre, but ignores the pawn on offer: White can settle the tension on its own terms and the knight move then achieves less than a capture that wins a tempo.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square and covers e5 and d4, the squares Black's knight and c-pawn would like to use. Nothing is committed yet: White can still choose between a positional squeeze and a kingside attack.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nc3.strategy: The usual way into the Grand Prix set-up: the knight guards e4 and watches d5 and b5, so the f-pawn can lead a kingside attack without leaving the centre loose. White keeps the g1 knight flexible and still chooses between a quiet squeeze and a direct assault.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Bc4.strategy: Aims the bishop at f7 at once, but gives Black an easy target: ...d5 hits the bishop with tempo, and the king's knight and castling are still waiting. White hurries the attack and gives Black comfortable development in return.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g6.strategy: The modern main line: Black fianchettoes the king's bishop to control the long diagonal and hit the centre from a distance instead of occupying it. It also keeps the king compact and the position sound against White's attacking set-up.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 e6.name: Sicilian Defence: McDonnell Attack
1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 e6.strategy: Prepares to challenge e4 with the d-pawn and opens the f8 bishop. A solid, flexible set-up: Black keeps the pawn structure compact and waits to see how White uses the f-pawn advance.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 d6.strategy: Supports the c5 pawn and the e5 square and lets the bishop on c8 out. A solid, flexible set-up, but it commits the d-pawn before Black knows how White plans to attack, and it is a quieter answer than the fianchetto.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 e6 4.d3.name: Sicilian Defence: McDonnell Attack
1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 e6 4.d3.strategy: Backs the e4 pawn and frees the c1 bishop. White chooses a restrained set-up, keeping the pawn centre compact and building towards a kingside attack rather than rushing it.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 e6 4.Bb5.strategy: Pressures the knight that holds d4 and e5 and threatens to double Black's pawns by taking it. White develops with a purpose and prepares to castle, keeping a positional squeeze in hand alongside the attack on the kingside.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 e6 4.c3.strategy: Prepares a broad pawn centre and denies the black knight the d4 square. The cost is that ...d5 hits e4 at once, and White usually answers by gaining space with e5, which closes the centre and fixes the pawns.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g6 4.Bb5.strategy: Attacks the knight that holds d4 and e5 and threatens to take it and double Black's pawns. A positional approach: White fights for the central squares first and has no need to hurry the kingside attack.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g6 4.Bc4.strategy: Aims the bishop at f7 and prepares to castle, choosing the direct kingside attack over a positional squeeze. The bishop is active, but Black's ...d5 break can hit it with tempo, so White must watch the centre.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g6 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the second knight, guards e4 and fights for d5, steering into the usual Grand Prix set-up. White decides nothing about the bishops yet and keeps both the positional and the aggressive plans available.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g6 4.Bb5 Bg7.name: Sicilian Defence: McDonnell Attack
1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g6 4.Bb5 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto and ignores the pressure on c6: the knight is guarded twice by pawns, and a trade would only give Black the bishop pair for doubled pawns. Meanwhile the bishop controls the long diagonal, including d4 and e5.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g6 4.Bb5 Nd4.strategy: Attacks both the bishop and the knight on f3 at once. If White trades on d4, the recapture with the c-pawn gives Black a pawn that cramps the centre and a lead in the fight for the dark squares; if not, the bishop has to be dealt with.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g6 4.Bb5 d6.strategy: Supports the c5 pawn and the e5 square and frees the c8 bishop. It leaves d7 empty, so Bxc6 comes with check and doubles Black's pawns for the bishop pair: a solid choice that hands White the easy decision.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g6 4.Bb5 Bg7 5.c3.strategy: Takes d4 away from the black knight, so ...Nd4 can no longer chase the bishop, and prepares a broad pawn centre. White keeps the bishop and the option of a big centre rather than trading it off, at the cost of a slower attack.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g6 4.Bb5 Bg7 5.Bx.strategy: Trades the bishop for the knight to double Black's pawns, but gives Black the bishop pair and, after the recapture, a half-open b-file. The doubled pawns are a lasting flaw, though not a decisive one, and White gives up the piece that was applying the pressure.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g6 4.Bb5 Bg7 5.O-.strategy: Completes the king's safety before the attack begins and leaves the bishop on b5 pressing on c6. The rook backs the f-pawn for a later advance, and White can still trade on c6 whenever it suits.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g6 4.Bb5 Bg7 5.Bx.strategy: Recaptures with the b-pawn, which keeps the d-pawn free to move and opens the b-file for a rook. The doubled c-pawns are a structural flaw, but Black has the bishop pair and a solid grip on the centre.

Recaptures with the d-pawn, which opens the diagonal of the c8 bishop and leaves the a- and b-pawns intact. The price is the d-pawn's grip on the centre: it can no longer come to d6 to cover e5, so White's e-pawn can gain space.
Ignores the recapture: the bishop on c6 is attacked by two pawns, but it simply retreats and White keeps the extra knight. Pressure on e4 is no compensation for a whole piece.
Brings the king to safety and the rook behind the advanced f-pawn, in line with White's kingside attacking plan, instead of spending time on the damaged black structure.
Supports e4 against the pressure of a coming knight on f6 and frees the c1 bishop. A restrained set-up that keeps the centre solid and lets White castle with the attack still in hand.
Guards e4 and eyes d5 and b5, the squares around Black's damaged queenside, while adding a piece to the centre. White develops quickly instead of rushing the f-pawn.
Backs the c5 pawn, covers e5 against White's f4 pawn and knight, and frees the bishop on c8. Black builds a compact, flexible pawn formation to put the doubled pawns to work in the centre.
Develops with an attack on the e4 pawn, which nothing defends, so White has to react at once. Black completes development with tempo and keeps the bishop pair.
Prepares to challenge the centre and keeps a compact structure, but it spends a move without developing a piece or covering e5, so White can seize space first.

1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g6 4.Bb5 Bg7 5.c3.name: Sicilian Defence: McDonnell Attack
1.e4 c5 2.f4 Nc6 3.Nf3 g6 4.Bb5 Bg7 5.c3.strategy: Develops and attacks the e4 pawn, which nothing defends. White must deal with it before the central plan can go ahead, while Black completes development with tempo.
Covers e5 and supports the c5 pawn, so White's central advance has little to aim at. Black develops calmly and keeps the king's side sound.

Asks the bishop what it intends: after a trade on c6 Black keeps the bishop pair, and after a retreat ...b5 gains queenside space with tempo. It spends a move away from development while e4 stays unpressured.
